passage: I'm Manjula, and I live in the flat below Devika's. This summer she asked her mother for one pot on their balcony, all to herself. She chose the seeds, tomato, from a packet at the market, and decided where the pot would go: the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested. Every morning I'd hear her little watering can, and sometimes her voice counting leaves. When the first flower came, she ran down the stairs to show me. When the first tomato turned red, she brought it to me on a steel plate, very serious. "I grew it. I picked the corner," she said. I don't know everything she was thinking, but she stood taller than I'd seen before.

qa.q: Where did Devika decide to put her pot?
qa.a: In the sunny corner, not the shady one her mother suggested.

qa.q: Why does Devika say "I picked the corner" so seriously?
qa.a: She is proud that her own choice worked; the red tomato shows her that what she decided made something happen.

qa.q: What choice by Devika's mother helped Devika learn that her actions matter?
qa.a: Letting Devika choose the seeds and the spot, even against her own suggestion, so the result clearly belonged to Devika.

qa.q: How does Manjula experience Devika's summer?
qa.a: Manjula hears the daily watering and gets shown every stage, and sees Devika standing taller, though only guessing at her thoughts.

grounding: A neighbour watches a child choose and tend a tomato plant and grow more confident when her choice works.

passage:
Saturday: Zubin's remote-control car stopped moving. He handed it to Afreen didi. "Fix it." "You fix it," she said, and gave him a small screwdriver. He poked at it for five minutes and gave up.
Monday: After school Zubin opened the car again, on his own this time. He found a wire loose from the battery box. He pushed it back and pressed it down with tape. The wheels twitched once, then stopped. He frowned, pressed harder, tried again. Whirr. The car shot across the floor.
Thursday: When his friend's torch stopped working, Zubin said, "Let me look," before anyone else could. He opened it, turned the batteries round, and it lit up. He grinned all the way home.

qa.q: What did Zubin find wrong with the car on Monday?
qa.a: A wire loose from the battery box.

qa.q: Why did Zubin say "Let me look" so quickly on Thursday?
qa.a: Fixing the car had shown him his efforts could work, so he felt confident and eager to try again.

qa.q: Which choice by Afreen didi helped Zubin most?
qa.a: Handing him the screwdriver instead of fixing it herself, so the success on Monday was his own.

qa.q: How might Afreen didi feel hearing about the torch on Thursday?
qa.a: She would probably be pleased that saying "You fix it" paid off, seeing her brother now step forward to fix things.

grounding: Over a week a child who fixes his own toy learns his actions matter and offers to fix a friend's torch.

passage: Mehak, come, look at this mango tree. When I was seven, I spat a mango seed into the corner of this yard and asked my father if I could keep it there. He said, "It's yours. You decide." So I decided everything. I put a ring of bricks round it so the goats wouldn't eat it. I carried water from the well in a small brass lota every evening, even when it rained, because I wasn't sure rain counted. When the first two leaves came up, I ran to tell everyone in the lane. Nobody else cared much, but I did. That's when I learned that if I did something, something happened. Disha's tree, they called it. Sixty years, and it still gives mangoes. Now, which pot do you want for your chilli seeds?

qa.q: What did young Disha put round the seed to protect it?
qa.a: A ring of bricks, so the goats wouldn't eat it.

qa.q: Why did young Disha keep watering even when it rained?
qa.a: Disha wasn't sure the rain counted and wanted to be certain the tree got its care; being in charge made every choice feel important.

qa.q: What choice by the father made the lesson possible?
qa.a: Saying "It's yours. You decide", which gave the child real decisions and a result to see.

qa.q: What might Mehak feel when asked to choose a pot for the chilli seeds?
qa.a: Mehak may feel trusted and excited, being handed the same kind of choice that made the mango tree so special.

grounding: An elder recalls how choosing and tending a mango seed as a child showed the child that actions could make things happen.

passage: Ujjwal's kite had torn on the neem tree, and there was no money for a new one before Sankranti. His grandfather, Kishore Dada, handed him a bowl of flour paste, old newspaper and thread. "Your kite. You decide how to fix it." The sun was already low. Ujjwal patched the hole with a big square of newspaper. On the roof the kite dipped and crashed. Too heavy on one side, he thought. He peeled half the patch off, cut a smaller one, and stuck a scrap on the other side to balance it. Dada said nothing, just held the spool. On the second try the kite wobbled, then climbed, steady, just before dark. Ujjwal stared up at it. "I did that," he whispered. "The patch did that."

qa.q: What did Kishore Dada hand Ujjwal?
qa.a: A bowl of flour paste, old newspaper and thread.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's whisper 'I did that' show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels proud and a bit amazed, seeing that his own decision about the patch is what made the kite fly.

qa.q: What choice by Kishore Dada helped Ujjwal learn that his actions matter?
qa.a: He let Ujjwal decide the repair and stayed quiet even after the crash, so the success clearly came from Ujjwal's own fix.

qa.q: What might Kishore Dada feel watching the kite climb?
qa.a: Probably quiet pride and pleasure, glad he held back his advice so Ujjwal could discover the fix himself.

grounding: A child who decides how to repair his torn kite, and sees it fly after his own adjustment, learns that his actions matter.

passage: In the Chennai flats, Farhan Uncle from the fourth floor gave Ganga, eight, an old plastic bottle made into a bird feeder. "Your job. You choose where it goes." Ganga hung it by the balcony door, where she could see it from her bed. For three days, no birds. Just ants. She sat on the step and thought. The pigeons liked the parapet; she'd seen them. The spot by the door was dark and next to the washing. So she moved the feeder to the sunny corner by the parapet and swept away the ants. On Saturday morning she shouted so loudly that Farhan Uncle looked up from the courtyard: two sparrows, pecking. "I moved it," she told him proudly. "That's why."

qa.q: Where did Ganga first hang the feeder?
qa.a: By the balcony door, where she could see it from her bed.

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking as she sat on the step after three days?
qa.a: She was puzzling out why no birds came, remembering the pigeons on the parapet and noticing that the first spot was dark and next to the washing.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference, and what did Ganga learn from it?
qa.a: Moving the feeder to the sunny corner by the parapet; when the sparrows came, she saw that her own decision had caused it.

qa.q: How might Farhan Uncle feel hearing 'I moved it. That's why'?
qa.a: Farhan Uncle would probably be delighted that giving Ganga the choice paid off, and see how proud she is of working it out herself 😊

grounding: A child chooses where to hang a bird feeder, moves it after it fails, and sees birds come because of her decision.
